Statics, Lesson 1

Friction

Until now, most of our problems came with supports that held firm. This lesson asks a different question: will the body stay where it is at all? The answer depends on friction, and on something a particle model hides, which is where the floor pushes back.

Eight sections, 20 interactive activities, and 50 in-class problems in two sets, placed where each topic comes up. Both are listed at the end of the page, so you can jump straight to any one. A scientific calculator opens from the Calculator button at the top of the page and on every in-class problem; you can drag it anywhere. Wherever you see a “Need a refresher?” button, it opens a short review of an earlier idea without leaving your place. Your progress on the checks is saved on this device.

Before you start

Two questions on ideas this lesson leans on. If either one is shaky, open the matching review below before going on.

1. Why friction matters

It is tempting to think of friction as waste: heat, wear, and lost energy. Sometimes it is. But take friction away and you cannot walk, a car cannot brake or steer, a ladder slides out from the wall, and every bolted joint in a steel building comes loose. Engineers spend as much effort getting enough friction as they do getting rid of it.

Try it: switch friction off

Three ordinary scenes, all standing still or working as expected. Predict what each one does when friction disappears, then turn it off.

The friction in this lesson is dry friction, also called Coulomb friction: the friction between solid surfaces with no lubricant between them (Hibbeler, 2022).

2. Three states of friction

Push gently on a heavy desk and it does not move. You are not weak; the floor is pushing back on the desk with a friction force exactly as large as your push. Push harder and friction grows to match. This is static friction, and the key fact about it is that it is a reaction. It takes whatever value equilibrium requires, up to a limit:

F ≤ μsN

Here F is the friction force, N is the normal force, and μs is the coefficient of static friction, a number with no units that depends on the two surfaces in contact.

At the limit, the body is on the verge of slipping. This state is called impending motion, and it is the only time you may write the friction force as an equation:

Fmax = μsN only at impending motion

Push past the limit and the body slides. Friction drops to the kinetic friction force, Fk = μkN, where μk is the coefficient of kinetic friction. For most pairs of surfaces μs is larger than μk, which is why a heavy garbage bag is harder to start dragging than to keep dragging (Beer et al., 2019).

Try it: quick fire

A new crate every time. Decide whether it is at rest or sliding, then enter the friction force. Watch for the crate nobody is pushing.

In class: the three states

Five problems on a level floor with a horizontal push. In each one, decide which state the crate is in before you write any friction equation.

Problem 1Crate on a rough floor with a horizontal push

A crate of mass m=35 kgm = 35\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45. A horizontal push PP is applied low on the crate so that tipping is not a concern. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the smallest horizontal push PP that will cause the crate to be on the verge of slipping.

Answer 155 N

Steps

  1. List the givens: m=35 kgm = 35\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.
  2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(35)(9.81)=343.35 NW = mg = (35)(9.81) = 343.35\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W=343.35 NN = W = 343.35\ \mathrm{N}.
  4. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: P=FP = F.
  5. Motion is impending, so the friction equation applies: F=μsNF = \mu_s N.
  6. Substitute: P=(0.45)(343.35 N)=154.5 NP = (0.45)(343.35\ \mathrm{N}) = 154.5\ \mathrm{N}
  7. State the result: P≈155 NP \approx 155\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=35 kgm = 35\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Weight: W=mg=(35 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=343.35 NW = mg = (35\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 343.35\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N−W=0N - W = 0, so N=343.35 NN = 343.35\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: P−F=0P - F = 0, so P=FP = F. At impending slip F=Fmax=μsNF = F_{max} = \mu_s N: P=μsN=(0.45)(343.35 N)=154.5 N≈155 NP = \mu_s N = (0.45)(343.35\ \mathrm{N}) = 154.5\ \mathrm{N} \approx 155\ \mathrm{N} Units: μs\mu_s is dimensionless, so the result is in newtons.

Problem 8Slowly increasing horizontal pull on a crate at impending slip

In a test, a crate of mass m=45 kgm = 45\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a horizontal concrete floor. A horizontal force applied low on the crate is increased slowly, and the crate is observed to be on the verge of slipping when the force reaches P=190 NP = 190\ \mathrm{N}. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the coefficient of static friction μs\mu_s between the crate and the floor.

Answer 0.430

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(45)(9.81)=441.45 NW = (45)(9.81) = 441.45\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=441.45 NN = 441.45\ \mathrm{N}.
  3. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=P=190 NF = P = 190\ \mathrm{N}.
  4. Slip is impending, so F=μsNF = \mu_s N.
  5. Solve for the coefficient: μs=190441.45=0.4304\mu_s = \frac{190}{441.45} = 0.4304
  6. State the result: μs≈0.430\mu_s \approx 0.430 (dimensionless).

Full solution

Given: m=45 kgm = 45\ \mathrm{kg}, P=190 NP = 190\ \mathrm{N} at impending slip. W=(45)(9.81)=441.45 NW = (45)(9.81) = 441.45\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=441.45 NN = 441.45\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=P=190 NF = P = 190\ \mathrm{N}. At impending motion F=Fmax=μsNF = F_{max} = \mu_s N, so μs=FmaxN=190 N441.45 N=0.4304≈0.430\mu_s = \frac{F_{max}}{N} = \frac{190\ \mathrm{N}}{441.45\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.4304 \approx 0.430 The newtons cancel, so μs\mu_s has no units.

Problem 2Crate pushed horizontally on a rough floor

A crate of mass m=50 kgm = 50\ \mathrm{kg} sits on a horizontal floor where μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40 and μk=0.30\mu_k = 0.30. A steady horizontal push of P=220 NP = 220\ \mathrm{N} is applied low on the crate. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Decide whether the crate stays at rest or slides, and determine the friction force that the floor actually exerts on the crate.

Answer 147 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight and normal force: N=W=(50)(9.81)=490.5 NN = W = (50)(9.81) = 490.5\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Find the static limit: Fmax=μsN=(0.40)(490.5)=196.2 NF_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.40)(490.5) = 196.2\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Friction required for equilibrium: F=P=220 NF = P = 220\ \mathrm{N}.
  4. Compare: 220 N>196.2 N220\ \mathrm{N} > 196.2\ \mathrm{N}, so the crate slips.
  5. Once sliding, use kinetic friction: Fk=μkN=(0.30)(490.5)=147.15 NF_k = \mu_k N = (0.30)(490.5) = 147.15\ \mathrm{N}
  6. State the result: the crate slides and F≈147 NF \approx 147\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=50 kgm = 50\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40, μk=0.30\mu_k = 0.30, P=220 NP = 220\ \mathrm{N}. W=mg=(50)(9.81)=490.5 NW = mg = (50)(9.81) = 490.5\ \mathrm{N} and ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0 gives N=490.5 NN = 490.5\ \mathrm{N}. Maximum static friction: Fmax=μsN=(0.40)(490.5 N)=196.2 NF_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.40)(490.5\ \mathrm{N}) = 196.2\ \mathrm{N}. Equilibrium would require F=P=220 NF = P = 220\ \mathrm{N}, which exceeds 196.2 N196.2\ \mathrm{N}, so static friction cannot hold the crate and it slides. While sliding, the friction force is kinetic: Fk=μkN=(0.30)(490.5 N)=147.15 N≈147 NF_k = \mu_k N = (0.30)(490.5\ \mathrm{N}) = 147.15\ \mathrm{N} \approx 147\ \mathrm{N}

Problem 23Friction force versus applied push, showing the drop at slipping

A crate of mass m=32 kgm = 32\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.42\mu_s = 0.42 and μk=0.33\mu_k = 0.33. A horizontal push is increased slowly until the crate breaks loose and begins to slide. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine how much the friction force drops at the instant the crate goes from impending motion to sliding.

Answer 28.3 N

Steps

  1. Compute the normal force: N=W=(32)(9.81)=313.92 NN = W = (32)(9.81) = 313.92\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Find the maximum static friction: Fmax=(0.42)(313.92)=131.85 NF_{max} = (0.42)(313.92) = 131.85\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Find the kinetic friction: Fk=(0.33)(313.92)=103.59 NF_k = (0.33)(313.92) = 103.59\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Take the difference: ΔF=(μs−μk)N=(0.09)(313.92)=28.25 N\Delta F = (\mu_s - \mu_k)N = (0.09)(313.92) = 28.25\ \mathrm{N}
  5. State the result: the friction force drops by about 28.3 N28.3\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=32 kgm = 32\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.42\mu_s = 0.42, μk=0.33\mu_k = 0.33. N=W=(32)(9.81)=313.92 NN = W = (32)(9.81) = 313.92\ \mathrm{N}. At impending motion: Fmax=μsN=(0.42)(313.92)=131.85 NF_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.42)(313.92) = 131.85\ \mathrm{N}. While sliding: Fk=μkN=(0.33)(313.92)=103.59 NF_k = \mu_k N = (0.33)(313.92) = 103.59\ \mathrm{N}. ΔF=Fmax−Fk=(μs−μk)N=(0.09)(313.92 N)=28.25 N≈28.3 N\Delta F = F_{max} - F_k = (\mu_s - \mu_k)N = (0.09)(313.92\ \mathrm{N}) = 28.25\ \mathrm{N} \approx 28.3\ \mathrm{N}

Problem 7Crate sliding at constant velocity under a horizontal push

A crate slides across a horizontal warehouse floor at constant velocity while a worker pushes on it with a horizontal force P=95.0 NP = 95.0\ \mathrm{N}. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is μk=0.28\mu_k = 0.28. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the mass of the crate.

Answer 34.6 kg

Steps

  1. Constant velocity means the crate is in equilibrium: ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0 and ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0.
  2. From ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: Fk=P=95.0 NF_k = P = 95.0\ \mathrm{N}.
  3. From ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=mgN = mg.
  4. The surfaces are sliding, so Fk=μkN=μkmgF_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k m g.
  5. Solve for the mass: m=Pμkg=95.0(0.28)(9.81)=34.59 kgm = \frac{P}{\mu_k g} = \frac{95.0}{(0.28)(9.81)} = 34.59\ \mathrm{kg}
  6. State the result: m≈34.6 kgm \approx 34.6\ \mathrm{kg}.

Full solution

Given: P=95.0 NP = 95.0\ \mathrm{N}, μk=0.28\mu_k = 0.28. Constant velocity means the forces balance. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: P−Fk=0P - F_k = 0, so Fk=95.0 NF_k = 95.0\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W=mgN = W = mg. While sliding, Fk=μkN=μkmgF_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k m g, so m=Pμkg=95.0 N(0.28)(9.81 m/s2)=34.59 kg≈34.6 kgm = \frac{P}{\mu_k g} = \frac{95.0\ \mathrm{N}}{(0.28)(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2})} = 34.59\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 34.6\ \mathrm{kg} Units: N/(m/s2)=kg\mathrm{N/(m/s^2) = kg}.

Second set: the same ideas with new numbers

Set 2, Problem 1Horizontal push at impending slip

A crate of mass m=42 kgm = 42\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is μs=0.38\mu_s = 0.38. A horizontal push PP is applied to the crate, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the magnitude of PP that places the crate on the verge of slipping. Assume the crate does not tip.

Determine the push PP at impending slip.

Answer 157 N

Steps

  1. Draw the free-body diagram: weight WW down, normal force NN up, push PP to the right, and friction FF to the left (opposing the tendency to slide).
  2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(42 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=412.0 NW = mg = (42\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 412.0\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N−W=0  ⇒  N=412.0 NN - W = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N = 412.0\ \mathrm{N}
  4. At impending slip, friction reaches its maximum value: F=Fmax=μsN=(0.38)(412.0 N)=156.6 NF = F_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.38)(412.0\ \mathrm{N}) = 156.6\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: P−F=0  ⇒  P=157 NP - F = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P = 157\ \mathrm{N}

Full solution

Given: m=42 kgm = 42\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.38\mu_s = 0.38, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Draw the free-body diagram: weight WW down, normal force NN up, push PP to the right, and friction FF to the left (opposing the tendency to slide).

2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(42 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=412.0 NW = mg = (42\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 412.0\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N−W=0  ⇒  N=412.0 NN - W = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N = 412.0\ \mathrm{N}

4. At impending slip, friction reaches its maximum value: F=Fmax=μsN=(0.38)(412.0 N)=156.6 NF = F_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.38)(412.0\ \mathrm{N}) = 156.6\ \mathrm{N}

5. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: P−F=0  ⇒  P=157 NP - F = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P = 157\ \mathrm{N}

Answer: 157 N157\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 8Measuring the static coefficient from a slip test

A crate of mass m1=58 kgm_1 = 58\ \mathrm{kg} carries a toolbox of mass m2=14 kgm_2 = 14\ \mathrm{kg} on top; the toolbox does not move relative to the crate. A horizontal pull PP on the crate is increased slowly from zero, as shown, and the crate first slips on the floor when P=265 NP = 265\ \mathrm{N}. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the coefficient of static friction μs\mu_s between the crate and the floor.

Determine the coefficient of static friction μs\mu_s.

Answer 0.375

Steps

  1. Treat the crate and toolbox as one body, since they move together. The floor supports the total weight.
  2. Compute the total weight: W=(m1+m2)g=(58+14) kg (9.81 m/s2)=706.3 NW = (m_1 + m_2)g = (58 + 14)\ \mathrm{kg}\,(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 706.3\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=706.3 NN = W = 706.3\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 at the instant of slip, where friction is at its maximum: Fmax=P=265 NF_{max} = P = 265\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Use Fmax=μsNF_{max} = \mu_s N: μs=FmaxN=265 N706.3 N=0.375\mu_s = \frac{F_{max}}{N} = \frac{265\ \mathrm{N}}{706.3\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.375
  6. State the result: μs=0.375\mu_s = 0.375, a dimensionless ratio of two forces.

Full solution

Given: m1=58 kgm_1 = 58\ \mathrm{kg}, m2=14 kgm_2 = 14\ \mathrm{kg}, slip at P=265 NP = 265\ \mathrm{N}, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Treat the crate and toolbox as one body, since they move together. The floor supports the total weight.

2. Compute the total weight: W=(m1+m2)g=(58+14) kg (9.81 m/s2)=706.3 NW = (m_1 + m_2)g = (58 + 14)\ \mathrm{kg}\,(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 706.3\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=706.3 NN = W = 706.3\ \mathrm{N}

4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 at the instant of slip, where friction is at its maximum: Fmax=P=265 NF_{max} = P = 265\ \mathrm{N}

5. Use Fmax=μsNF_{max} = \mu_s N: μs=FmaxN=265 N706.3 N=0.375\mu_s = \frac{F_{max}}{N} = \frac{265\ \mathrm{N}}{706.3\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.375

6. State the result: μs=0.375\mu_s = 0.375, a dimensionless ratio of two forces.

Answer: 0.375

Set 2, Problem 2Does it slide? Static check, then kinetic friction

A crate of mass m=65 kgm = 65\ \mathrm{kg} is at rest on a rough horizontal floor with μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45 and μk=0.35\mu_k = 0.35. A horizontal push P=300 NP = 300\ \mathrm{N} is then applied, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Decide whether the crate remains at rest or slides, and determine the magnitude of the friction force FF that acts on the crate under this push.

Determine the friction force FF acting on the crate.

Answer 223 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight and the normal force from ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mg=(65 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=637.6 NN = W = mg = (65\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 637.6\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Compute the maximum static friction available: Fmax=μsN=(0.45)(637.6 N)=286.9 NF_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.45)(637.6\ \mathrm{N}) = 286.9\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Compare with the force needed for equilibrium, F=P=300 NF = P = 300\ \mathrm{N}: since 300 N>286.9 N300\ \mathrm{N} > 286.9\ \mathrm{N}, static friction cannot hold the crate and it slides.
  4. Once sliding, the friction is kinetic: F=Fk=μkN=(0.35)(637.6 N)=223.2 NF = F_k = \mu_k N = (0.35)(637.6\ \mathrm{N}) = 223.2\ \mathrm{N}
  5. State the result: the crate slides and F=223 NF = 223\ \mathrm{N}, directed opposite to the motion.

Full solution

Given: m=65 kgm = 65\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45, μk=0.35\mu_k = 0.35, P=300 NP = 300\ \mathrm{N}, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Compute the weight and the normal force from ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mg=(65 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=637.6 NN = W = mg = (65\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 637.6\ \mathrm{N}

2. Compute the maximum static friction available: Fmax=μsN=(0.45)(637.6 N)=286.9 NF_{max} = \mu_s N = (0.45)(637.6\ \mathrm{N}) = 286.9\ \mathrm{N}

3. Compare with the force needed for equilibrium, F=P=300 NF = P = 300\ \mathrm{N}: since 300 N>286.9 N300\ \mathrm{N} > 286.9\ \mathrm{N}, static friction cannot hold the crate and it slides.

4. Once sliding, the friction is kinetic: F=Fk=μkN=(0.35)(637.6 N)=223.2 NF = F_k = \mu_k N = (0.35)(637.6\ \mathrm{N}) = 223.2\ \mathrm{N}

5. State the result: the crate slides and F=223 NF = 223\ \mathrm{N}, directed opposite to the motion.

Answer: 223 N223\ \mathrm{N}

3. Compute the level after slipping, the kinetic friction: Fk=μkN=(0.37)(431.6 N)=159.7 NF_k = \mu_k N = (0.37)(431.6\ \mathrm{N}) = 159.7\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 7Constant-velocity sliding and kinetic friction

A crate slides across a rough horizontal floor at constant velocity under a horizontal push P=132 NP = 132\ \mathrm{N}, as shown. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is μk=0.24\mu_k = 0.24. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the mass mm of the crate.

Determine the mass mm of the crate.

Answer 56.1 kg

Steps

  1. Recognize that constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the equilibrium equations apply with kinetic friction Fk=μkNF_k = \mu_k N.
  2. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: P−Fk=0  ⇒  Fk=132 NP - F_k = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; F_k = 132\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Use Fk=μkNF_k = \mu_k N to find the normal force: N=Fkμk=132 N0.24=550 NN = \frac{F_k}{\mu_k} = \frac{132\ \mathrm{N}}{0.24} = 550\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mgN = W = mg, so m=Ng=550 N9.81 m/s2=56.07 kgm = \frac{N}{g} = \frac{550\ \mathrm{N}}{9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}} = 56.07\ \mathrm{kg}
  5. State the result: m=56.1 kgm = 56.1\ \mathrm{kg}.

Full solution

Given: P=132 NP = 132\ \mathrm{N}, μk=0.24\mu_k = 0.24, constant velocity, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Recognize that constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the equilibrium equations apply with kinetic friction Fk=μkNF_k = \mu_k N.

2. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: P−Fk=0  ⇒  Fk=132 NP - F_k = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; F_k = 132\ \mathrm{N}

3. Use Fk=μkNF_k = \mu_k N to find the normal force: N=Fkμk=132 N0.24=550 NN = \frac{F_k}{\mu_k} = \frac{132\ \mathrm{N}}{0.24} = 550\ \mathrm{N}

4. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mgN = W = mg, so m=Ng=550 N9.81 m/s2=56.07 kgm = \frac{N}{g} = \frac{550\ \mathrm{N}}{9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}} = 56.07\ \mathrm{kg}

5. State the result: m=56.1 kgm = 56.1\ \mathrm{kg}.

Answer: 56.1 kg56.1\ \mathrm{kg}

Two details people get wrong

The coefficient is not a force. μs is a ratio. The force needed to start a body sliding on a level floor is μsN, which depends on how hard the surfaces are pressed together.

Friction does not always oppose the motion of the object. It opposes sliding between the two surfaces, or the tendency to slide. When you walk, your shoe pushes backward on the floor. Friction on your shoe points forward, the same direction you are moving. To find the direction, ask which way the surface would slide if friction vanished, and point friction the other way.

Try it: which way does friction act?

Seven cases. In each one, decide the direction before you choose, then see the arrow drawn.

Problem 17Forces on a worker pushing a crate

A worker of mass m=75 kgm = 75\ \mathrm{kg} stands on a level floor and pushes horizontally on a heavy crate with a force of 250 N250\ \mathrm{N}. The crate does not move, and the worker’s feet do not slide. Treat the worker as a body acted on by the crate’s horizontal reaction, the worker’s weight, and the floor’s normal and friction forces. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction between the worker’s shoes and the floor that keeps the worker from slipping.

Answer 0.340

Steps

  1. The crate pushes back on the worker with R=250 NR = 250\ \mathrm{N}.
  2. Find the friction direction: the shoes would slide backward without friction, so FF on the shoes points forward.
  3. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=250 NF = 250\ \mathrm{N}.
  4. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=(75)(9.81)=735.75 NN = (75)(9.81) = 735.75\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Impose the no-slip condition F≤μsNF \le \mu_s N: μs,min=250735.75=0.3398\mu_{s,min} = \frac{250}{735.75} = 0.3398
  6. State the result: μs≥0.340\mu_s \ge 0.340.

Full solution

Given: m=75 kgm = 75\ \mathrm{kg}, push =250 N= 250\ \mathrm{N}. By Newton’s third law the crate pushes back on the worker with R=250 NR = 250\ \mathrm{N}. Without friction the shoes would slide backward, so friction on the shoes points forward, toward the crate. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=R=250 NF = R = 250\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W=(75)(9.81)=735.75 NN = W = (75)(9.81) = 735.75\ \mathrm{N}. No slipping requires F≤μsNF \le \mu_s N, so μs,min=FN=250 N735.75 N=0.3398≈0.340\mu_{s,min} = \frac{F}{N} = \frac{250\ \mathrm{N}}{735.75\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.3398 \approx 0.340

Problem 25Resultant of the normal and friction forces at impending slip

A crate of mass m=40 kgm = 40\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.50\mu_s = 0.50. A horizontal push applied low on the crate is increased until slipping is impending. At that instant the floor exerts on the crate both a normal force NN and a friction force FF, which combine into a single resultant contact force RR. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the magnitude of the resultant contact force RR that the floor exerts on the crate at impending slip.

Answer 439 N

Steps

  1. Compute the normal force: N=W=(40)(9.81)=392.4 NN = W = (40)(9.81) = 392.4\ \mathrm{N}
  2. At impending slip use F=μsNF = \mu_s N: F=(0.50)(392.4)=196.2 NF = (0.50)(392.4) = 196.2\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Combine the perpendicular components: R=N2+F2=N1+μs2R = \sqrt{N^2 + F^2} = N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}
  4. Substitute: R=(392.4)1.25=438.7 NR = (392.4)\sqrt{1.25} = 438.7\ \mathrm{N}
  5. State the result: R≈439 NR \approx 439\ \mathrm{N}, tilted from the normal by ϕs=tan⁡−1(μs)\phi_s = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s).

Full solution

Given: m=40 kgm = 40\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.50\mu_s = 0.50. N=W=(40)(9.81)=392.4 NN = W = (40)(9.81) = 392.4\ \mathrm{N}. At impending slip: F=μsN=(0.50)(392.4)=196.2 NF = \mu_s N = (0.50)(392.4) = 196.2\ \mathrm{N}. NN and FF are perpendicular, so R=N2+F2=N1+μs2=(392.4 N)1+0.25=438.7 N≈439 NR = \sqrt{N^2 + F^2} = N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2} = (392.4\ \mathrm{N})\sqrt{1 + 0.25} = 438.7\ \mathrm{N} \approx 439\ \mathrm{N} RR is inclined from the normal by the angle of static friction, ϕs=tan⁡−1(0.50)=26.6∘\phi_s = \tan^{-1}(0.50) = 26.6^{\circ}.

Second set: the same ideas with new numbers

Set 2, Problem 17Friction needed under a worker pushing a crate

The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is μc=0.24\mu_c = 0.24, and the crate slips before it tips. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction μw\mu_w between the worker’s shoes and the floor that allows the worker to bring the crate to the verge of slipping without the shoes slipping.

Determine the minimum shoe–floor coefficient μw\mu_w.

Answer 0.360

Steps

  1. Draw separate free-body diagrams. On the crate, friction FcF_c opposes the push. On the worker, the crate pushes back with PP (Newton’s third law), so floor friction FwF_w on the shoes acts forward, toward the crate.
  2. Crate, ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: Nc=mcg=(120 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=1177 NN_c = m_c g = (120\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 1177\ \mathrm{N}

  4. Worker, ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: Nw=mwg=(80 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=784.8 NN_w = m_w g = (80\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 784.8\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Worker, ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: Fw=P=282.5 NF_w = P = 282.5\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 25Resultant contact force at impending slip

A crate of mass m=52 kgm = 52\ \mathrm{kg} on a rough horizontal floor is pushed horizontally until slipping is impending. The coefficient of static friction is μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35. The floor’s normal force NN and friction force FF combine into a single resultant contact force RR, tilted at the angle ϕs\phi_s from the normal, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the magnitude of RR.

Determine the magnitude of the resultant contact force RR.

Answer 540 N

Steps

  1. Compute the normal force from ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mg=(52 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=510.1 NN = W = mg = (52\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 510.1\ \mathrm{N}

  3. Combine the perpendicular components: R=N2+F2=N1+μs2R = \sqrt{N^2 + F^2} = N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}
  4. Substitute: R=(510.1 N)1+(0.35)2=(510.1 N)(1.059)=540.5 NR = (510.1\ \mathrm{N})\sqrt{1 + (0.35)^2} = (510.1\ \mathrm{N})(1.059) = 540.5\ \mathrm{N}
  5. State the result: R=540 NR = 540\ \mathrm{N}, tilted from the normal by the angle of static friction ϕs=tan⁡−1(0.35)=19.3∘\phi_s = \tan^{-1}(0.35) = 19.3^{\circ}.

Full solution

Given: m=52 kgm = 52\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Compute the normal force from ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N=W=mg=(52 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=510.1 NN = W = mg = (52\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 510.1\ \mathrm{N}

2. At impending slip the friction is at its maximum: F=μsN=(0.35)(510.1 N)=178.5 NF = \mu_s N = (0.35)(510.1\ \mathrm{N}) = 178.5\ \mathrm{N}

3. Combine the perpendicular components: R=N2+F2=N1+μs2R = \sqrt{N^2 + F^2} = N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}

4. Substitute: R=(510.1 N)1+(0.35)2=(510.1 N)(1.059)=540.5 NR = (510.1\ \mathrm{N})\sqrt{1 + (0.35)^2} = (510.1\ \mathrm{N})(1.059) = 540.5\ \mathrm{N}

Answer: 540 N540\ \mathrm{N}

When the push or pull is angled

So far the normal force has equaled the weight. That is true only when nothing else pushes or pulls vertically. A push angled downward presses the body into the floor and raises N, which raises the friction available. A pull angled upward lifts some of the weight off the floor and lowers both. Always get N from ΣFy = 0. Never assume N = W.

Try it. Swing the force from a downward push to an upward pull and watch N change. Then push at 70° with μs = 0.40 and try to make the crate slip.

Problem 16Downward-angled push increases the normal force

A crate of mass m=28 kgm = 28\ \mathrm{kg} rests in equilibrium on a horizontal floor. A worker leans on it with a force P=90.0 NP = 90.0\ \mathrm{N} directed at θ=40∘\theta = 40^{\circ} below the horizontal. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the normal force NN that the floor exerts on the crate.

Answer 333 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(28)(9.81)=274.68 NW = (28)(9.81) = 274.68\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Find the vertical component of the push: Psin⁡θ=(90.0)sin⁡40∘=57.85 NP\sin\theta = (90.0)\sin 40^{\circ} = 57.85\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N−W−Psin⁡θ=0N - W - P\sin\theta = 0.
  4. Substitute: N=274.68+57.85=332.5 NN = 274.68 + 57.85 = 332.5\ \mathrm{N}
  5. State the result: N≈333 NN \approx 333\ \mathrm{N}, larger than the weight.

Full solution

Given: m=28 kgm = 28\ \mathrm{kg}, P=90.0 NP = 90.0\ \mathrm{N}, θ=40∘\theta = 40^{\circ}. W=(28)(9.81)=274.68 NW = (28)(9.81) = 274.68\ \mathrm{N}. The vertical component of the push is Psin⁡θ=(90.0)sin⁡40∘=57.85 NP\sin\theta = (90.0)\sin 40^{\circ} = 57.85\ \mathrm{N}, downward. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N−W−Psin⁡θ=0N - W - P\sin\theta = 0, so N=274.68 N+57.85 N=332.5 N≈333 NN = 274.68\ \mathrm{N} + 57.85\ \mathrm{N} = 332.5\ \mathrm{N} \approx 333\ \mathrm{N}

Problem 3Crate pushed by a force angled below the horizontal

A crate of mass m=40 kgm = 40\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35. A worker pushes on it with a force PP directed at θ=25∘\theta = 25^{\circ} below the horizontal. The crate is low and wide, so tipping does not occur. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the magnitude of PP for which slipping is impending.

Answer 181 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(40)(9.81)=392.4 NW = (40)(9.81) = 392.4\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Write ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: Pcos⁡θ=FP\cos\theta = F.
  3. Write ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta (the downward push increases NN).
  4. Apply the impending-slip condition F=μsNF = \mu_s N: Pcos⁡θ=μs(W+Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s (W + P\sin\theta)
  5. Solve for PP: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s \sin\theta}
  6. Substitute: P=(0.35)(392.4)cos⁡25∘−0.35sin⁡25∘=137.340.7584 NP = \frac{(0.35)(392.4)}{\cos 25^{\circ} - 0.35\sin 25^{\circ}} = \frac{137.34}{0.7584}\ \mathrm{N}
  7. State the result: P≈181 NP \approx 181\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=40 kgm = 40\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35, θ=25∘\theta = 25^{\circ}. W=(40)(9.81)=392.4 NW = (40)(9.81) = 392.4\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: Pcos⁡θ−F=0P\cos\theta - F = 0. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N−W−Psin⁡θ=0N - W - P\sin\theta = 0, so N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta. Impending slip: F=μsNF = \mu_s N. Combining: Pcos⁡θ=μs(W+Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s (W + P\sin\theta), so P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θ=(0.35)(392.4 N)0.9063−(0.35)(0.4226)=137.34 N0.7584=181.1 N≈181 NP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s \sin\theta} = \frac{(0.35)(392.4\ \mathrm{N})}{0.9063 - (0.35)(0.4226)} = \frac{137.34\ \mathrm{N}}{0.7584} = 181.1\ \mathrm{N} \approx 181\ \mathrm{N} The denominator is dimensionless, so PP is in newtons.

Problem 14Crate pulled by a rope angled above the horizontal

A crate of mass m=55 kgm = 55\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.30\mu_s = 0.30. A rope attached low on the crate pulls with a tension PP directed at θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ} above the horizontal. Tipping does not occur. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the rope tension PP at which slipping is impending.

Answer 159 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(55)(9.81)=539.55 NW = (55)(9.81) = 539.55\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Write ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: Pcos⁡θ=FP\cos\theta = F.
  3. Write ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W−Psin⁡θN = W - P\sin\theta (the upward pull reduces NN).
  4. Apply impending slip, F=μsNF = \mu_s N: Pcos⁡θ=μs(W−Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s(W - P\sin\theta)
  5. Solve for PP: P=μsWcos⁡θ+μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta}
  6. Substitute: P=161.870.8660+0.1500=159.3 NP = \frac{161.87}{0.8660 + 0.1500} = 159.3\ \mathrm{N}
  7. State the result: P≈159 NP \approx 159\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=55 kgm = 55\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.30\mu_s = 0.30, θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ}. W=(55)(9.81)=539.55 NW = (55)(9.81) = 539.55\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: Pcos⁡θ=FP\cos\theta = F. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N+Psin⁡θ−W=0N + P\sin\theta - W = 0, so N=W−Psin⁡θN = W - P\sin\theta. Impending slip: F=μsNF = \mu_s N, so Pcos⁡θ=μs(W−Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s(W - P\sin\theta) and P=μsWcos⁡θ+μssin⁡θ=(0.30)(539.55 N)0.8660+(0.30)(0.5000)=161.87 N1.0160=159.3 N≈159 NP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta} = \frac{(0.30)(539.55\ \mathrm{N})}{0.8660 + (0.30)(0.5000)} = \frac{161.87\ \mathrm{N}}{1.0160} = 159.3\ \mathrm{N} \approx 159\ \mathrm{N}

Problem 24Steeply angled push on a crate

A crate rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. A worker pushes on it with a force PP directed at an angle θ\theta below the horizontal. As θ\theta increases, more of the push goes into pressing the crate against the floor. Tipping does not occur.

Determine the angle θ\theta at and beyond which no push, however large, can make the crate slip.

Answer 68.2 deg

Steps

  1. Write ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=Pcos⁡θF = P\cos\theta.
  2. Write ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta.
  3. Apply impending slip, F=μsNF = \mu_s N, and solve for PP: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}
  4. Note that PP becomes unbounded when the denominator reaches zero.
  5. Set cos⁡θ−μssin⁡θ=0\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta = 0: tan⁡θ=1μs=2.5\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\mu_s} = 2.5
  6. State the result: θ≈68.2∘\theta \approx 68.2^{\circ}; at this angle or steeper the crate cannot be pushed into slipping.

Full solution

Given: μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. Let the crate have weight WW. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=Pcos⁡θF = P\cos\theta. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta. Impending slip, F=μsNF = \mu_s N, gives P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta} As the denominator approaches zero, the required PP grows without limit. Setting cos⁡θ−μssin⁡θ=0\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta = 0: tan⁡θ=1μs=10.40=2.5,θ=68.2∘\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\mu_s} = \frac{1}{0.40} = 2.5, \quad \theta = 68.2^{\circ} At this angle and steeper, each added newton of push adds at least as much available friction as it adds horizontal force, so the crate cannot be made to slip.

Full solution

Given: m=36 kgm = 36\ \mathrm{kg}, P=120 NP = 120\ \mathrm{N} at θ=35∘\theta = 35^{\circ} below horizontal, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Compute the weight: W=mg=(36 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=353.2 NW = mg = (36\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 353.2\ \mathrm{N}

2. Find the vertical component of the push, which acts downward: Psin⁡θ=(120 N)sin⁡35∘=68.83 NP\sin\theta = (120\ \mathrm{N})\sin 35^{\circ} = 68.83\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: N−W−Psin⁡θ=0N - W - P\sin\theta = 0

4. Solve and substitute: N=W+Psin⁡θ=353.2 N+68.83 N=422.0 NN = W + P\sin\theta = 353.2\ \mathrm{N} + 68.83\ \mathrm{N} = 422.0\ \mathrm{N}

5. State the result: N=422 NN = 422\ \mathrm{N}, larger than the weight.

Answer: 422 N422\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 3Push angled below the horizontal

A crate of mass m=48 kgm = 48\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a rough horizontal floor with μs=0.32\mu_s = 0.32. A worker pushes on it with a force PP directed at θ=28∘\theta = 28^{\circ} below the horizontal, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the magnitude of PP required to bring the crate to the verge of slipping. Assume the crate does not tip.

Determine the push PP at impending slip.

Answer 206 N

Steps

  1. Draw the free-body diagram and resolve the push: Pcos⁡θP\cos\theta acts to the right and Psin⁡θP\sin\theta acts downward, pressing the crate into the floor.
  2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(48 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=470.9 NW = mg = (48\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 470.9\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0; the normal force is not equal to the weight: N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta
  4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 with F=μsNF = \mu_s N at impending slip: Pcos⁡θ=μs (W+Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s\,(W + P\sin\theta)
  5. Solve for PP: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}
  6. Substitute: P=(0.32)(470.9 N)cos⁡28∘−(0.32)sin⁡28∘=150.7 N0.7327=205.6 NP = \frac{(0.32)(470.9\ \mathrm{N})}{\cos 28^{\circ} - (0.32)\sin 28^{\circ}} = \frac{150.7\ \mathrm{N}}{0.7327} = 205.6\ \mathrm{N}
  7. State the result and check: P=206 NP = 206\ \mathrm{N}, with N=567.4 N>WN = 567.4\ \mathrm{N} > W as expected for a downward-angled push.

Full solution

Given: m=48 kgm = 48\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.32\mu_s = 0.32, θ=28∘\theta = 28^{\circ} below horizontal, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Draw the free-body diagram and resolve the push: Pcos⁡θP\cos\theta acts to the right and Psin⁡θP\sin\theta acts downward, pressing the crate into the floor.

2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(48 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=470.9 NW = mg = (48\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 470.9\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0; the normal force is not equal to the weight: N=W+Psin⁡θN = W + P\sin\theta

4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 with F=μsNF = \mu_s N at impending slip: Pcos⁡θ=μs (W+Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s\,(W + P\sin\theta)

5. Solve for PP: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}

6. Substitute: P=(0.32)(470.9 N)cos⁡28∘−(0.32)sin⁡28∘=150.7 N0.7327=205.6 NP = \frac{(0.32)(470.9\ \mathrm{N})}{\cos 28^{\circ} - (0.32)\sin 28^{\circ}} = \frac{150.7\ \mathrm{N}}{0.7327} = 205.6\ \mathrm{N}

7. State the result and check: P=206 NP = 206\ \mathrm{N}, with N=567.4 N>WN = 567.4\ \mathrm{N} > W as expected for a downward-angled push.

Answer: 206 N206\ \mathrm{N}

Given: m=70 kgm = 70\ \mathrm{kg}, μs=0.34\mu_s = 0.34, θ=22∘\theta = 22^{\circ} above horizontal, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

1. Resolve the pull: Pcos⁡θP\cos\theta acts to the right and Psin⁡θP\sin\theta acts upward, partly lifting the crate.

2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(70 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=686.7 NW = mg = (70\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 686.7\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 24Steep push angle beyond which no push causes slip

A crate of weight WW rests on a rough horizontal floor with μs=0.55\mu_s = 0.55. A push PP is applied at an angle θ\theta below the horizontal, as shown. As θ\theta is made steeper, the push needed to cause slipping grows without bound. Determine the angle θ\theta at and beyond which no push, however large, can make the crate slip.

Determine the limiting push angle θ\theta.

Answer 61.2 deg

Steps

  1. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 and ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: F=Pcos⁡θ,N=W+Psin⁡θF = P\cos\theta, \qquad N = W + P\sin\theta
  2. Set F=μsNF = \mu_s N at impending slip and solve for the push: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}
  3. Observe that P→∞P \to \infty as the denominator approaches zero; beyond that point the push adds more to the available friction than to the driving force.
  4. Set the denominator to zero: cos⁡θ−μssin⁡θ=0  ⇒  tan⁡θ=1μs\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{1}{\mu_s}
  5. Substitute: θ=tan⁡−1 ⁣(10.55)=tan⁡−1(1.818)=61.2∘\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{0.55}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1.818) = 61.2^{\circ}
  6. State the result: for θ≥61.2∘\theta \ge 61.2^{\circ} the crate cannot be made to slip. The weight cancels, so the angle depends only on μs\mu_s.

Full solution

Given: μs=0.55\mu_s = 0.55; push at angle θ\theta below the horizontal.

Solution:

1. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 and ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: F=Pcos⁡θ,N=W+Psin⁡θF = P\cos\theta, \qquad N = W + P\sin\theta

2. Set F=μsNF = \mu_s N at impending slip and solve for the push: P=μsWcos⁡θ−μssin⁡θP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}

3. Observe that P→∞P \to \infty as the denominator approaches zero; beyond that point the push adds more to the available friction than to the driving force.

4. Set the denominator to zero: cos⁡θ−μssin⁡θ=0  ⇒  tan⁡θ=1μs\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{1}{\mu_s}

5. Substitute: θ=tan⁡−1 ⁣(10.55)=tan⁡−1(1.818)=61.2∘\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{0.55}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1.818) = 61.2^{\circ}

6. State the result: for θ≥61.2∘\theta \ge 61.2^{\circ} the crate cannot be made to slip. The weight cancels, so the angle depends only on μs\mu_s.

Answer: 61.2∘61.2^{\circ}

3. Free-body diagrams with friction

In a physics course a crate is usually a particle, and the normal force is drawn through its center. A real crate is a rigid body, and the floor’s push is spread across the whole base. We replace that spread-out push with a single resultant N, and its location is one of the unknowns.

Consider a crate of weight W and base width a, pushed by a horizontal force P at height h. Four forces act on it: P, W straight down through the center of gravity, friction F along the floor, and N at some distance x from the centerline. Equilibrium gives:

ΣFx = 0:   P − F = 0 so F = P

ΣFy = 0:   N − W = 0 so N = W

ΣMO = 0:   Nx − Ph = 0 so x = Ph/W, taking moments about O, the middle of the base

The push tries to rotate the crate forward. The only thing that can resist is N moving toward the front edge. The harder or higher you push, the farther it moves. But N cannot act outside the base. When x reaches a/2 the crate is about to tip.

So equilibrium needs two conditions at once:

  • No slipping: F ≤ μsN
  • No tipping: x ≤ a/2

Try it: build the free-body diagram

Eight candidate forces, four of which belong. Each one you select is drawn on the crate.

Try it: balance the crate

Before the figure does it for you, do it yourself. Drag the green normal force along the base, or use the slider, until the moments about O cancel. Then select “New push” and predict where N must go before you move it.

Use Figure 2 to try three things. Raise P slowly and watch N walk toward the edge. Lower the push height and see the tipping limit move away. Then use the three floor buttons: the same crate under the same growing push slides on a polished floor and falls over on a rubber mat. More grip did not make the crate safer. It changed how the crate fails.

In class: where the normal force acts

Problem 4Free-body diagram with the normal force offset by x

A crate of mass m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg} rests in equilibrium on a rough horizontal floor. A horizontal push P=120 NP = 120\ \mathrm{N} is applied at a height h=0.90 mh = 0.90\ \mathrm{m} above the floor. Let OO be the midpoint of the base and let xx be the distance from OO to the line of action of the resultant normal force NN. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the offset distance xx of the normal force from the centerline.

Answer 0.183 m

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 NW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W=588.6 NN = W = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}.
  3. Take moments about OO, the middle of the base: Nx−Ph=0Nx - Ph = 0
  4. Solve for the offset: x=PhWx = \frac{Ph}{W}
  5. Substitute: x=(120)(0.90)588.6=0.1835 mx = \frac{(120)(0.90)}{588.6} = 0.1835\ \mathrm{m}
  6. State the result: x≈0.183 mx \approx 0.183\ \mathrm{m} toward the front edge.

Full solution

Given: m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg}, P=120 NP = 120\ \mathrm{N}, h=0.90 mh = 0.90\ \mathrm{m}. W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 NW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=W=588.6 NN = W = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}. ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0: Nx−Ph=0Nx - Ph = 0, so x=PhW=(120 N)(0.90 m)588.6 N=0.1835 m≈0.183 mx = \frac{Ph}{W} = \frac{(120\ \mathrm{N})(0.90\ \mathrm{m})}{588.6\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.1835\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.183\ \mathrm{m} Units: N⋅m/N=m\mathrm{N \cdot m / N = m}. The normal force shifts toward the edge the crate would tip about.

Problem 22Normal-force offset compared with the half-width of the base

A uniform crate of mass m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg} has a base of width a=0.80 ma = 0.80\ \mathrm{m} and rests in equilibrium on a rough floor. A horizontal push P=150 NP = 150\ \mathrm{N} is applied at a height h=1.00 mh = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}. A stability gauge reports how much of the tipping limit has been used, defined as the ratio of the normal-force offset xx to its limiting value a/2a/2, expressed as a percentage. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the percentage of the tipping limit that this push has used.

Answer 63.7 %

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 N,N=WW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}, \quad N = W
  2. Take moments about OO: Nx−Ph=0Nx - Ph = 0.
  3. Solve for the offset: x=(150)(1.00)588.6=0.2548 mx = \frac{(150)(1.00)}{588.6} = 0.2548\ \mathrm{m}
  4. Identify the tipping limit: a/2=0.40 ma/2 = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}.
  5. Form the ratio: xa/2⋅100=0.25480.40⋅100=63.7 %\frac{x}{a/2} \cdot 100 = \frac{0.2548}{0.40} \cdot 100 = 63.7\ \%
  6. State the result: about 63.7 %63.7\ \% of the tipping limit is used, so the crate does not tip.

Full solution

Given: m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg}, a=0.80 ma = 0.80\ \mathrm{m}, P=150 NP = 150\ \mathrm{N}, h=1.00 mh = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}. W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 NW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N} and N=WN = W. ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0: Nx−Ph=0Nx - Ph = 0, so x=(150 N)(1.00 m)588.6 N=0.2548 mx = \dfrac{(150\ \mathrm{N})(1.00\ \mathrm{m})}{588.6\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.2548\ \mathrm{m}. The tipping limit is a/2=0.40 ma/2 = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}. xa/2⋅100=0.2548 m0.40 m⋅100=63.7 %\frac{x}{a/2} \cdot 100 = \frac{0.2548\ \mathrm{m}}{0.40\ \mathrm{m}} \cdot 100 = 63.7\ \% Since the ratio is below 100 %100\ \%, the crate is not tipping.

Problem 5Crate on the verge of tipping about its front edge

A uniform crate of mass m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg} has a base of width a=0.80 ma = 0.80\ \mathrm{m}. It is pushed horizontally at a height h=1.20 mh = 1.20\ \mathrm{m} above the floor. The floor is rough enough that the crate does not slip. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the push PP at which tipping is impending.

Answer 196 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 NW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}
  2. State the tipping condition: NN acts at the edge, x=a/2=0.40 mx = a/2 = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}.
  3. Use ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=WN = W.
  4. Take moments about the middle of the base: N(a2)−Ph=0N\left(\frac{a}{2}\right) - Ph = 0
  5. Solve and substitute: P=(588.6)(0.40)1.20=196.2 NP = \frac{(588.6)(0.40)}{1.20} = 196.2\ \mathrm{N}
  6. State the result: P≈196 NP \approx 196\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=60 kgm = 60\ \mathrm{kg}, a=0.80 ma = 0.80\ \mathrm{m}, h=1.20 mh = 1.20\ \mathrm{m}. W=(60)(9.81)=588.6 NW = (60)(9.81) = 588.6\ \mathrm{N}. At impending tipping the normal force acts at the front edge, x=a/2=0.40 mx = a/2 = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}. From ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0: Nx−Ph=0Nx - Ph = 0 with N=WN = W: P=W(a/2)h=(588.6 N)(0.40 m)1.20 m=196.2 N≈196 NP = \frac{W(a/2)}{h} = \frac{(588.6\ \mathrm{N})(0.40\ \mathrm{m})}{1.20\ \mathrm{m}} = 196.2\ \mathrm{N} \approx 196\ \mathrm{N} Units: N⋅m/m=N\mathrm{N \cdot m / m = N}.

Problem 12Angled push on a crate with the normal force at unknown position x

A uniform crate of mass m=30 kgm = 30\ \mathrm{kg} has a base of width 1.00 m1.00\ \mathrm{m} and rests in equilibrium on a rough horizontal floor. A force P=120 NP = 120\ \mathrm{N} pushes on its left face, directed to the right and downward at θ=20∘\theta = 20^{\circ} below the horizontal. The force is applied 0.50 m0.50\ \mathrm{m} to the left of the crate’s centerline and 0.30 m0.30\ \mathrm{m} above the floor. Let OO be the midpoint of the base and let xx be the position of the resultant normal force NN measured from OO, positive to the right. Nothing says motion is impending. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solve the equilibrium equations and determine the position xx of the normal force.

Answer 0.0397 m

Steps

  1. Identify the type: no apparent impending motion, so solve for FF, NN, and xx from equilibrium alone.
  2. Compute the weight: W=(30)(9.81)=294.3 NW = (30)(9.81) = 294.3\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Resolve the push: Pcos⁡20∘=112.76 NP\cos 20^{\circ} = 112.76\ \mathrm{N} and Psin⁡20∘=41.04 NP\sin 20^{\circ} = 41.04\ \mathrm{N}.
  4. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=112.76 NF = 112.76\ \mathrm{N}.
  5. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=294.3+41.04=335.34 NN = 294.3 + 41.04 = 335.34\ \mathrm{N}
  6. Take moments about OO: (41.04)(0.50)−(112.76)(0.30)+Nx=0(41.04)(0.50) - (112.76)(0.30) + Nx = 0
  7. Solve: x=33.83−20.52335.34=0.0397 mx = \frac{33.83 - 20.52}{335.34} = 0.0397\ \mathrm{m}
  8. State the result: NN acts 0.0397 m0.0397\ \mathrm{m} to the right of the centerline, inside the base, so there is no tipping.

Full solution

Given: m=30 kgm = 30\ \mathrm{kg}, P=120 NP = 120\ \mathrm{N}, θ=20∘\theta = 20^{\circ}. W=(30)(9.81)=294.3 NW = (30)(9.81) = 294.3\ \mathrm{N}. Components of PP: Pcos⁡θ=112.76 NP\cos\theta = 112.76\ \mathrm{N} (right), Psin⁡θ=41.04 NP\sin\theta = 41.04\ \mathrm{N} (down). ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: F=112.76 NF = 112.76\ \mathrm{N}. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: N=294.3+41.04=335.34 NN = 294.3 + 41.04 = 335.34\ \mathrm{N}. ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0 (counterclockwise positive): (41.04 N)(0.50 m)−(112.76 N)(0.30 m)+Nx=0(41.04\ \mathrm{N})(0.50\ \mathrm{m}) - (112.76\ \mathrm{N})(0.30\ \mathrm{m}) + Nx = 0, so x=33.83−20.52335.34 m=0.0397 mx = \frac{33.83 - 20.52}{335.34}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.0397\ \mathrm{m} The positive sign means NN acts about 40 mm40\ \mathrm{mm} to the right of the centerline, well inside the 0.50 m0.50\ \mathrm{m} half-width, so the crate does not tip.

Set 2, Problem 22Fraction of the tipping limit in use

A crate of mass m=85 kgm = 85\ \mathrm{kg} and base width a=0.90 ma = 0.90\ \mathrm{m} rests on a rough floor and does not slip. A horizontal push P=210 NP = 210\ \mathrm{N} is applied at a height h=1.15 mh = 1.15\ \mathrm{m} above the floor, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Set 2, Problem 5Push at impending tipping

A crate of mass m=90 kgm = 90\ \mathrm{kg} and base width a=0.70 ma = 0.70\ \mathrm{m} rests on a floor rough enough to prevent slipping. Determine the push PP at impending tipping.

4. Slip or tip? A procedure

When you do not know which failure comes first, assume one, solve, and check the other.

  1. Draw the free-body diagram. Show F opposing the tendency to slide and N at an unknown distance x.
  2. Assume one kind of impending motion. For slipping, add F = μsN. For tipping, set x = a/2.
  3. Solve the three equilibrium equations with that one extra condition.
  4. Check the other condition. If you assumed slipping, is x ≤ a/2? If you assumed tipping, is F ≤ μsN?
  5. If the check fails, your assumption was wrong. Switch and solve again. The motion that needs the smaller force governs.

Call it: slip or tip?

Each round deals a new crate. Decide, as a class or on your own, what happens first as the push grows. Then find out. After a few rounds, look for the shortcut: which two numbers are you really comparing?

Worked Example A: horizontal push, US customary units

A crate weighs W = 250 lb and has a base 3 ft wide. A worker pushes horizontally at a height of 5 ft. The coefficient of static friction is 0.40. What is the largest push that causes no motion?

Assume slipping. N = W = 250 lb, so

P = F = μsN = (0.40)(250 lb) = 100 lb

Check tipping.

x = Ph/W = (100 lb)(5 ft)/(250 lb) = 2.0 ft

But a/2 = 1.5 ft. The normal force would have to act outside the base, which is impossible. The assumption fails: the crate tips before it slips.

Assume tipping. Set x = 1.5 ft.

P = Wx/h = (250 lb)(1.5 ft)/(5 ft) = 75 lb

Check slipping. F = P = 75 lb, which is less than μsN = 100 lb. The check passes.

Answer. The largest push is 75 lb, and tipping governs.

Worked Example B: angled push, SI units

A uniform crate has a mass of 20 kg and a base 0.8 m wide. A force P = 80 N pushes on it at 30° below the horizontal. The force is applied 0.4 m to the left of the crate’s centerline and 0.2 m above the floor. The coefficient of static friction is 0.3. Does the crate stay in equilibrium? (After Hibbeler, 2022, Example 8.1.)

Here nothing says motion is impending, so there are three unknowns (F, N, x) and three equilibrium equations. Solve first, then check both limits. W = (20 kg)(9.81 m/s²) = 196.2 N.

ΣFx = 0:   (80 N) cos 30° − F = 0,   F = 69.3 N

ΣFy = 0:   N − (80 N) sin 30° − 196.2 N = 0,   N = 236.2 N

ΣMO = 0:   (40 N)(0.4 m) − (69.3 N)(0.2 m) + Nx = 0,   x = −0.00908 m

Check tipping. The negative sign means N acts about 9 mm to the left of the centerline. That is far inside the 0.4 m half-width, so the crate does not tip.

Check slipping. Fmax = μsN = (0.3)(236.2 N) = 70.9 N. The 69.3 N required is less than that, so the crate does not slip.

Answer. The crate stays in equilibrium, though it is close to slipping. Notice that pushing downward raised N, and with it the available friction.

Try it: spot the error

Five short solutions, each with exactly one wrong line. These are the mistakes that cost the most points on friction problems.

Practice: as many as you want

Each problem has new numbers. Work it on paper, enter your answer, and check it. The feedback looks for the usual slips, such as reporting the other limit or using mass in place of weight.

In class: slip or tip

Problem 6Slip-or-tip free-body diagram of a pushed crate

A uniform crate of mass m=80 kgm = 80\ \mathrm{kg} has a base of width a=0.60 ma = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}. A worker pushes horizontally at a height h=1.00 mh = 1.00\ \mathrm{m} above the floor. The coefficient of static friction is μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35. It is not known in advance whether the crate will slip or tip first. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Using the assume-solve-check procedure, determine the largest push PP that causes no motion, and identify whether slipping or tipping governs.

Answer 235 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(80)(9.81)=784.8 N,N=WW = (80)(9.81) = 784.8\ \mathrm{N}, \quad N = W
  2. Assume slipping: P=μsN=(0.35)(784.8)=274.7 NP = \mu_s N = (0.35)(784.8) = 274.7\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Check tipping for that push: x=PhW=(274.7)(1.00)784.8=0.350 mx = \frac{Ph}{W} = \frac{(274.7)(1.00)}{784.8} = 0.350\ \mathrm{m}
  4. Compare with a/2=0.30 ma/2 = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}: x>a/2x > a/2 is impossible, so the slipping assumption fails.
  5. Assume tipping with x=a/2x = a/2: P=W(a/2)h=(784.8)(0.30)1.00=235.4 NP = \frac{W(a/2)}{h} = \frac{(784.8)(0.30)}{1.00} = 235.4\ \mathrm{N}
  6. Check slipping: F=235.4 N≤274.7 NF = 235.4\ \mathrm{N} \le 274.7\ \mathrm{N}, so the check passes.
  7. State the result: Pmax≈235 NP_{max} \approx 235\ \mathrm{N}, and tipping governs.

Full solution

Given: m=80 kgm = 80\ \mathrm{kg}, a=0.60 ma = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}, h=1.00 mh = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}, μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35. W=(80)(9.81)=784.8 NW = (80)(9.81) = 784.8\ \mathrm{N}, N=WN = W. Assume slipping: P=F=μsN=(0.35)(784.8 N)=274.7 NP = F = \mu_s N = (0.35)(784.8\ \mathrm{N}) = 274.7\ \mathrm{N}. Check tipping: x=Ph/W=(274.7)(1.00)/784.8=0.350 mx = Ph/W = (274.7)(1.00)/784.8 = 0.350\ \mathrm{m}, but a/2=0.30 ma/2 = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}, so NN would lie outside the base. The assumption fails. Assume tipping: x=a/2=0.30 mx = a/2 = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}, so P=W(a/2)h=(784.8 N)(0.30 m)1.00 m=235.4 N≈235 NP = \frac{W(a/2)}{h} = \frac{(784.8\ \mathrm{N})(0.30\ \mathrm{m})}{1.00\ \mathrm{m}} = 235.4\ \mathrm{N} \approx 235\ \mathrm{N} Check slipping: F=P=235.4 N≤μsN=274.7 NF = P = 235.4\ \mathrm{N} \le \mu_s N = 274.7\ \mathrm{N}. The check passes, so tipping governs.

Problem 11Push height that separates slipping from tipping

A uniform crate with a base of width a=0.70 ma = 0.70\ \mathrm{m} rests on a horizontal floor where μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. A horizontal push is applied at a height hh above the floor and increased slowly.

Determine the push height hh at which slipping and tipping become impending at the same time. (Pushes below this height make the crate slip first; pushes above it make the crate tip first.)

Answer 0.875 m

Steps

  1. Write the slipping push: Pslip=μsWP_{slip} = \mu_s W.
  2. Write the tipping push from ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0 with x=a/2x = a/2: Ptip=W(a/2)hP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{h}
  3. Set the two equal for simultaneous impending motion: μsW=Wa2h\mu_s W = \frac{W a}{2h}
  4. Solve for hh: h=a2μsh = \frac{a}{2\mu_s}
  5. Substitute: h=0.702(0.40)=0.875 mh = \frac{0.70}{2(0.40)} = 0.875\ \mathrm{m}
  6. State the result: h=0.875 mh = 0.875\ \mathrm{m}.

Full solution

Given: a=0.70 ma = 0.70\ \mathrm{m}, μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. Slipping is impending when P=μsN=μsWP = \mu_s N = \mu_s W. Tipping is impending when x=a/2x = a/2, which from ΣMO=0\Sigma M_O = 0 gives P=W(a/2)/hP = W(a/2)/h. Setting the two equal: μsW=Wa/(2h)\mu_s W = W a/(2h), so h=a2μs=0.70 m2(0.40)=0.875 mh = \frac{a}{2\mu_s} = \frac{0.70\ \mathrm{m}}{2(0.40)} = 0.875\ \mathrm{m} The weight cancels, so the result holds for any crate mass.

Problem 18Rope pulling at the top corner of a crate

A uniform crate of mass m=50 kgm = 50\ \mathrm{kg} has a base of width a=0.60 ma = 0.60\ \mathrm{m} and a height H=1.00 mH = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}. A rope attached to its top right corner CC pulls with tension PP directed up and to the right at θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ} above the horizontal. The lower right corner is BB. The coefficient of static friction is μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the largest tension PP that causes no motion, and identify whether slipping or tipping governs.

Answer 170 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(50)(9.81)=490.5 NW = (50)(9.81) = 490.5\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Assume slipping with N=W−Psin⁡θN = W - P\sin\theta and F=μsNF = \mu_s N: P=μsWcos⁡θ+μssin⁡θ=196.21.0660=184.0 NP = \frac{\mu_s W}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta} = \frac{196.2}{1.0660} = 184.0\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Assume tipping: NN and FF act at corner BB.
  4. Take moments about BB; the vertical component of PP passes through BB: Wa2−(Pcos⁡θ)H=0W\frac{a}{2} - (P\cos\theta)H = 0
  5. Solve: P=(490.5)(0.30)(1.00)cos⁡30∘=169.9 NP = \frac{(490.5)(0.30)}{(1.00)\cos 30^{\circ}} = 169.9\ \mathrm{N}
  6. Check slipping at this load: F=147.2 N≤μsN=(0.40)(405.5)=162.2 NF = 147.2\ \mathrm{N} \le \mu_s N = (0.40)(405.5) = 162.2\ \mathrm{N}.
  7. State the result: Pmax≈170 NP_{max} \approx 170\ \mathrm{N}, and tipping governs.

Full solution

Given: m=50 kgm = 50\ \mathrm{kg}, a=0.60 ma = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}, H=1.00 mH = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}, θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ}, μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. W=(50)(9.81)=490.5 NW = (50)(9.81) = 490.5\ \mathrm{N}. Assume slipping: Pcos⁡θ=μs(W−Psin⁡θ)P\cos\theta = \mu_s(W - P\sin\theta), so P=(0.40)(490.5)0.8660+(0.40)(0.5000)=196.21.0660=184.0 NP = \dfrac{(0.40)(490.5)}{0.8660 + (0.40)(0.5000)} = \dfrac{196.2}{1.0660} = 184.0\ \mathrm{N}. Assume tipping about BB: NN and FF act at BB, and the vertical component of PP passes through BB because CC is directly above BB. ΣMB=0\Sigma M_B = 0: W(a/2)−(Pcos⁡θ)H=0W(a/2) - (P\cos\theta)H = 0, so P=W(a/2)Hcos⁡θ=(490.5 N)(0.30 m)(1.00 m)(0.8660)=169.9 N≈170 NP = \frac{W(a/2)}{H\cos\theta} = \frac{(490.5\ \mathrm{N})(0.30\ \mathrm{m})}{(1.00\ \mathrm{m})(0.8660)} = 169.9\ \mathrm{N} \approx 170\ \mathrm{N} The smaller force governs. Check slipping at P=169.9 NP = 169.9\ \mathrm{N}: F=Pcos⁡θ=147.2 NF = P\cos\theta = 147.2\ \mathrm{N}, N=490.5−84.96=405.5 NN = 490.5 - 84.96 = 405.5\ \mathrm{N}, μsN=162.2 N≥147.2 N\mu_s N = 162.2\ \mathrm{N} \ge 147.2\ \mathrm{N}. The check passes, so tipping governs.

Full solution

Given: m=110 kgm = 110\ \mathrm{kg}, a=0.90 ma = 0.90\ \mathrm{m}, h=1.10 mh = 1.10\ \mathrm{m}, μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Compute the weight; ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0 gives N=WN = W: W=mg=(110 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=1079 NW = mg = (110\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 1079\ \mathrm{N}

2. Assume slipping: F=μsNF = \mu_s N and ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 give Pslip=μsW=(0.45)(1079 N)=485.6 NP_{slip} = \mu_s W = (0.45)(1079\ \mathrm{N}) = 485.6\ \mathrm{N}

3. Check the assumption with ∑MO=0\sum M_O = 0: x=Pslip hW=(485.6 N)(1.10 m)1079 N=0.495 mx = \frac{P_{slip}\,h}{W} = \frac{(485.6\ \mathrm{N})(1.10\ \mathrm{m})}{1079\ \mathrm{N}} = 0.495\ \mathrm{m}

4. Compare with the half-width: x=0.495 m>a/2=0.450 mx = 0.495\ \mathrm{m} > a/2 = 0.450\ \mathrm{m}, so NN would lie outside the base. The slip assumption fails; the crate tips first.

5. Assume tipping about AA (x=a/2x = a/2) and apply ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0: Ptip=W(a/2)h=(1079 N)(0.450 m)1.10 m=441.5 NP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{h} = \frac{(1079\ \mathrm{N})(0.450\ \mathrm{m})}{1.10\ \mathrm{m}} = 441.5\ \mathrm{N}

6. Check friction: F=Ptip=441.5 N≤μsN=485.6 NF = P_{tip} = 441.5\ \mathrm{N} \le \mu_s N = 485.6\ \mathrm{N}, so the crate does not slip.

7. State the result: P=441 NP = 441\ \mathrm{N}, and tipping governs.

Answer: 441 N441\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 11Push height separating slipping from tipping

A uniform crate with base width a=0.90 ma = 0.90\ \mathrm{m} rests on a rough horizontal floor with μs=0.36\mu_s = 0.36. A horizontal push PP is applied at height hh above the floor, as shown. Determine the height hh at which the crate is simultaneously on the verge of slipping and on the verge of tipping. Pushes below this height make the crate slip first; pushes above it make the crate tip first.

Determine the critical push height hh.

Answer 1.25 m

Steps

  1. Write the push that causes slipping: ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0 gives N=WN = W, and F=μsNF = \mu_s N gives Pslip=μsWP_{slip} = \mu_s W
  2. Write the push that causes tipping about the front edge AA, from ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0: Ptip=W(a/2)hP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{h}
  3. Set the two pushes equal at the transition height: μsW=Wa2h\mu_s W = \frac{W a}{2h}
  4. Cancel the weight and solve for hh: h=a2μsh = \frac{a}{2\mu_s}
  5. Substitute: h=0.90 m2(0.36)=0.90 m0.720=1.25 mh = \frac{0.90\ \mathrm{m}}{2(0.36)} = \frac{0.90\ \mathrm{m}}{0.720} = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}
  6. State the result: h=1.25 mh = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}, valid for a crate of any mass because WW cancels.

Full solution

Given: a=0.90 ma = 0.90\ \mathrm{m}, μs=0.36\mu_s = 0.36.

Solution:

1. Write the push that causes slipping: ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0 gives N=WN = W, and F=μsNF = \mu_s N gives Pslip=μsWP_{slip} = \mu_s W

2. Write the push that causes tipping about the front edge AA, from ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0: Ptip=W(a/2)hP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{h}

3. Set the two pushes equal at the transition height: μsW=Wa2h\mu_s W = \frac{W a}{2h}

4. Cancel the weight and solve for hh: h=a2μsh = \frac{a}{2\mu_s}

5. Substitute: h=0.90 m2(0.36)=0.90 m0.720=1.25 mh = \frac{0.90\ \mathrm{m}}{2(0.36)} = \frac{0.90\ \mathrm{m}}{0.720} = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}

6. State the result: h=1.25 mh = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}, valid for a crate of any mass because WW cancels.

Answer: 1.25 m1.25\ \mathrm{m}

Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the smallest tension PP that causes the crate to move, and state whether it slips or tips.

Determine the smallest tension PP that causes motion (identify slipping or tipping).

Answer 202 N

Steps

Solve for the tipping tension: Ptip=W(a/2)Hcos⁡θ=(627.8 N)(0.350 m)(1.20 m)cos⁡25∘=219.7 N⋅m1.088 m=202.1 NP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{H\cos\theta} = \frac{(627.8\ \mathrm{N})(0.350\ \mathrm{m})}{(1.20\ \mathrm{m})\cos 25^{\circ}} = \frac{219.7\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}}{1.088\ \mathrm{m}} = 202.1\ \mathrm{N}

Solve for the tipping tension: Ptip=W(a/2)Hcos⁡θ=(627.8 N)(0.350 m)(1.20 m)cos⁡25∘=219.7 N⋅m1.088 m=202.1 NP_{tip} = \frac{W(a/2)}{H\cos\theta} = \frac{(627.8\ \mathrm{N})(0.350\ \mathrm{m})}{(1.20\ \mathrm{m})\cos 25^{\circ}} = \frac{219.7\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}}{1.088\ \mathrm{m}} = 202.1\ \mathrm{N}
