5. Three types of friction problems

Once the free-body diagrams are drawn, count the unknowns and compare them with the equations you have: three equilibrium equations per rigid body, plus one friction equation for each contact where slipping is impending (Hibbeler, 2022).

Table 1Types of Dry-Friction Problems
TypeCountWhat you do
No apparent impending motionUnknowns = equilibrium equationsSolve with equilibrium alone, then check F ≤ μsN at every contact. Worked Example B is this type.
Impending motion at all points of contactUnknowns = equilibrium equations + friction equationsUse F = μsN at every contact and solve everything together.
Impending motion at some points of contactUnknowns < equilibrium equations + possible friction or tipping equationsSeveral motions are possible. Assume one, solve, and check, as in the slip-or-tip procedure. Worked Example A is this type.

Try it: name the type

Seven short problem statements. Do not solve them. Decide which of the three types each one is.

Practice: a bar against a wall

A uniform bar weighing 100 N leans against a wall. The coefficient of static friction is 0.3 at the floor (point A) and 0.4 at the wall (point B). Find the smallest angle θ between the bar and the floor at which the bar will not slip. Work it on paper before stepping through the solution.

Slipping is impending at both contacts, so this is the second type: five unknowns (NA, FA, NB, FB, θ), three equilibrium equations, and two friction equations. The bottom of the bar tends to slide away from the wall, so FA points toward the wall. The top tends to slide down, so FB points up.

FA = 0.3NA,   FB = 0.4NB

ΣFx = 0:   NB = FA = 0.3NA

ΣFy = 0:   NA + 0.4(0.3NA) = 100 N,   NA = 89.3 N

So NB = 26.8 N and FB = 10.7 N. Taking moments about A for a bar of length L:

(100 N)(L/2) cos θ = (26.8 N)L sin θ + (10.7 N)L cos θ

tan θ = (50 − 10.7)/26.8 = 1.467,   θ = 55.7°

The length cancels. At any angle steeper than 55.7° the bar stays put.

Try it: how far can the bar lean?

Set the two coefficients from the practice problem (0.30 at the floor, 0.40 at the wall) and lower the bar until it lets go. Then make the wall smooth and see how much the limit moves.

In class: a bar against a wall

Problem 9Bar leaning against a rough wall on a rough floor

A uniform bar of weight W=150 NW = 150\ \mathrm{N} leans against a vertical wall. Its lower end AA rests on the floor, where μA=0.25\mu_A = 0.25, and its upper end BB rests against the wall, where μB=0.35\mu_B = 0.35. The bar makes an angle θ\theta with the floor.

Determine the smallest angle θ\theta at which the bar will not slip.

Answer 61.3 deg

Steps

  1. Identify the type: slipping is impending at both AA and BB, so FA=0.25NAF_A = 0.25N_A and FB=0.35NBF_B = 0.35N_B.
  2. Set directions: FAF_A points toward the wall and FBF_B points up.
  3. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: NB=FA=0.25NAN_B = F_A = 0.25N_A.
  4. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: NA+(0.35)(0.25)NA=150 N⇒NA=137.9 NN_A + (0.35)(0.25)N_A = 150\ \mathrm{N} \Rightarrow N_A = 137.9\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Compute NB=34.48 NN_B = 34.48\ \mathrm{N} and FB=12.07 NF_B = 12.07\ \mathrm{N}.
  6. Take moments about AA: WL2cos⁡θ=NBLsin⁡θ+FBLcos⁡θW\frac{L}{2}\cos\theta = N_B L\sin\theta + F_B L\cos\theta
  7. Solve: tan⁡θ=75−12.0734.48=1.825\tan\theta = \frac{75 - 12.07}{34.48} = 1.825
  8. State the result: θ≈61.3∘\theta \approx 61.3^{\circ}; any steeper angle is safe.

Full solution

Slipping is impending at both contacts: FA=0.25NAF_A = 0.25N_A (toward the wall) and FB=0.35NBF_B = 0.35N_B (upward). ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: NB=FA=0.25NAN_B = F_A = 0.25N_A. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: NA+FB=WN_A + F_B = W, so NA+(0.35)(0.25NA)=150 NN_A + (0.35)(0.25N_A) = 150\ \mathrm{N}, giving NA=150/1.0875=137.9 NN_A = 150/1.0875 = 137.9\ \mathrm{N}. Then NB=(0.25)(137.9)=34.48 NN_B = (0.25)(137.9) = 34.48\ \mathrm{N} and FB=(0.35)(34.48)=12.07 NF_B = (0.35)(34.48) = 12.07\ \mathrm{N}. Moments about AA for a bar of length LL: W(L/2)cos⁡θ=NBLsin⁡θ+FBLcos⁡θW(L/2)\cos\theta = N_B L\sin\theta + F_B L\cos\theta, so tan⁡θ=W/2−FBNB=75−12.0734.48=1.825,θ=61.3∘\tan\theta = \frac{W/2 - F_B}{N_B} = \frac{75 - 12.07}{34.48} = 1.825, \quad \theta = 61.3^{\circ} The length cancels, and the ratio of forces is dimensionless.

Second set: the same ideas with new numbers

Set 2, Problem 9Bar against a rough wall on a rough floor

A uniform bar ABAB of weight W=220 NW = 220\ \mathrm{N} and length LL leans against a rough vertical wall at BB with its lower end AA on a rough horizontal floor, as shown. The coefficients of static friction are μA=0.30\mu_A = 0.30 at the floor and μB=0.20\mu_B = 0.20 at the wall. Determine the smallest angle θ\theta between the bar and the floor for which the bar remains in equilibrium, with slipping impending at both AA and BB.

Determine the smallest angle θ\theta for equilibrium.

Answer 57.4 deg

Steps

  1. Establish friction directions: end AA tends to slide away from the wall, so FAF_A acts toward the wall; end BB tends to slide down, so FBF_B acts upward. With slip impending at both ends, FA=μANAF_A = \mu_A N_A and FB=μBNBF_B = \mu_B N_B.
  2. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: FA−NB=0  ⇒  NB=μANAF_A - N_B = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_B = \mu_A N_A
  3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: NA+FB−W=0  ⇒  NA+μBμANA=WN_A + F_B - W = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_A + \mu_B \mu_A N_A = W
  4. Solve for the floor reaction: NA=W1+μAμB=220 N1.06=207.5 NN_A = \frac{W}{1 + \mu_A \mu_B} = \frac{220\ \mathrm{N}}{1.06} = 207.5\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Compute the wall forces: NB=(0.30)(207.5 N)=62.26 N,FB=(0.20)(62.26 N)=12.45 NN_B = (0.30)(207.5\ \mathrm{N}) = 62.26\ \mathrm{N}, \qquad F_B = (0.20)(62.26\ \mathrm{N}) = 12.45\ \mathrm{N}
  6. Apply ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0: W L2cos⁡θ=NBLsin⁡θ+FBLcos⁡θW\,\frac{L}{2}\cos\theta = N_B L \sin\theta + F_B L \cos\theta
  7. Divide by Lcos⁡θL\cos\theta and solve; the length cancels: tan⁡θ=W/2−FBNB=110 N−12.45 N62.26 N=1.567\tan\theta = \frac{W/2 - F_B}{N_B} = \frac{110\ \mathrm{N} - 12.45\ \mathrm{N}}{62.26\ \mathrm{N}} = 1.567
  8. State the result: θ=tan⁡−1(1.567)=57.4∘\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.567) = 57.4^{\circ}. Any steeper angle is safe.

Full solution

Given: W=220 NW = 220\ \mathrm{N}, μA=0.30\mu_A = 0.30 (floor), μB=0.20\mu_B = 0.20 (wall), slip impending at both ends.

Solution:

1. Establish friction directions: end AA tends to slide away from the wall, so FAF_A acts toward the wall; end BB tends to slide down, so FBF_B acts upward. With slip impending at both ends, FA=μANAF_A = \mu_A N_A and FB=μBNBF_B = \mu_B N_B.

2. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0: FA−NB=0  ⇒  NB=μANAF_A - N_B = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_B = \mu_A N_A

3. Apply ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: NA+FB−W=0  ⇒  NA+μBμANA=WN_A + F_B - W = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_A + \mu_B \mu_A N_A = W

4. Solve for the floor reaction: NA=W1+μAμB=220 N1.06=207.5 NN_A = \frac{W}{1 + \mu_A \mu_B} = \frac{220\ \mathrm{N}}{1.06} = 207.5\ \mathrm{N}

5. Compute the wall forces: NB=(0.30)(207.5 N)=62.26 N,FB=(0.20)(62.26 N)=12.45 NN_B = (0.30)(207.5\ \mathrm{N}) = 62.26\ \mathrm{N}, \qquad F_B = (0.20)(62.26\ \mathrm{N}) = 12.45\ \mathrm{N}

6. Apply ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0: W L2cos⁡θ=NBLsin⁡θ+FBLcos⁡θW\,\frac{L}{2}\cos\theta = N_B L \sin\theta + F_B L \cos\theta

7. Divide by Lcos⁡θL\cos\theta and solve; the length cancels: tan⁡θ=W/2−FBNB=110 N−12.45 N62.26 N=1.567\tan\theta = \frac{W/2 - F_B}{N_B} = \frac{110\ \mathrm{N} - 12.45\ \mathrm{N}}{62.26\ \mathrm{N}} = 1.567

8. State the result: θ=tan⁡−1(1.567)=57.4∘\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.567) = 57.4^{\circ}. Any steeper angle is safe.

Answer: 57.4∘57.4^{\circ}

6. Put it to work: the painter’s ladder

The bar against the wall is a ladder, and the practical question is how far up it someone can climb. As the painter climbs, the load moves toward the wall, the wall pushes back harder, and the floor has to supply more friction to match. At some height the floor runs out.

Predict first: if the painter gets halfway up safely, are they safe the rest of the way?

Try three changes and explain each with a free-body diagram: stand the ladder steeper, roughen the floor, and roughen the wall. Which one buys the most height?

Problem 19Bar against a smooth wall on a rough floor

A uniform bar leans against a smooth (frictionless) vertical wall. Its lower end AA rests on a rough horizontal floor, and its upper end BB touches the wall. The bar makes an angle θ=60∘\theta = 60^{\circ} with the floor and is in equilibrium.

Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction at AA required to hold the bar in this position.

Answer 0.289

Steps

  1. Draw the free-body diagram: WW at midlength, NAN_A and FAF_A at the floor, and only NBN_B at the smooth wall.
  2. Apply ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: NA=WN_A = W.
  3. Apply ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: FA=NBF_A = N_B.
  4. Take moments about AA: WL2cos⁡θ=NBLsin⁡θ⇒NB=W2tan⁡θW\frac{L}{2}\cos\theta = N_B L\sin\theta \Rightarrow N_B = \frac{W}{2\tan\theta}
  5. Impose FA≤μsNAF_A \le \mu_s N_A: μs,min=12tan⁡θ\mu_{s,min} = \frac{1}{2\tan\theta}
  6. Substitute: μs,min=12tan⁡60∘=0.289\mu_{s,min} = \frac{1}{2\tan 60^{\circ}} = 0.289
  7. State the result: μs≥0.289\mu_s \ge 0.289 at the floor.

Full solution

Let the bar have weight WW and length LL. The wall is smooth, so only NBN_B acts at BB. ΣFy=0\Sigma F_y = 0: NA=WN_A = W. ΣFx=0\Sigma F_x = 0: FA=NBF_A = N_B. ΣMA=0\Sigma M_A = 0: W(L/2)cos⁡θ−NBLsin⁡θ=0W(L/2)\cos\theta - N_B L\sin\theta = 0, so NB=W2tan⁡θN_B = \dfrac{W}{2\tan\theta}. The friction required is FA=W2tan⁡θF_A = \dfrac{W}{2\tan\theta}, and no slipping requires FA≤μsNAF_A \le \mu_s N_A: μs,min=FANA=12tan⁡θ=12tan⁡60∘=13.464=0.289\mu_{s,min} = \frac{F_A}{N_A} = \frac{1}{2\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{2\tan 60^{\circ}} = \frac{1}{3.464} = 0.289 Both WW and LL cancel.

Second set: the same ideas with new numbers

Set 2, Problem 19Pole against a smooth wall on a rough floor

A uniform thin pole ABAB of mass m=14 kgm = 14\ \mathrm{kg} and length L=6.5 mL = 6.5\ \mathrm{m} leans against a smooth vertical wall at BB. Its lower end AA rests on a rough horizontal floor at a distance d=2.5 md = 2.5\ \mathrm{m} from the wall, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction μs\mu_s at the floor for which the pole remains in this position when released.

Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction μs\mu_s at the floor.

Answer 0.208

Steps

  1. Find the height of BB above the floor from the right triangle: hB=L2−d2=(6.5 m)2−(2.5 m)2=6.00 mh_B = \sqrt{L^2 - d^2} = \sqrt{(6.5\ \mathrm{m})^2 - (2.5\ \mathrm{m})^2} = 6.00\ \mathrm{m}
  2. Compute the weight, which acts at midlength, a horizontal distance d/2d/2 from AA: W=mg=(14 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=137.3 NW = mg = (14\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 137.3\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0; the smooth wall exerts only a horizontal force NBN_B: W(d2)−NB hB=0  ⇒  NB=(137.3 N)(1.25 m)6.00 m=28.61 NW\left(\frac{d}{2}\right) - N_B\,h_B = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_B = \frac{(137.3\ \mathrm{N})(1.25\ \mathrm{m})}{6.00\ \mathrm{m}} = 28.61\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 and ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: FA=NB=28.61 N,NA=W=137.3 NF_A = N_B = 28.61\ \mathrm{N}, \qquad N_A = W = 137.3\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Require FA≤μsNAF_A \le \mu_s N_A; the minimum coefficient is μs=FANA=28.61 N137.3 N=d2hB=0.208\mu_s = \frac{F_A}{N_A} = \frac{28.61\ \mathrm{N}}{137.3\ \mathrm{N}} = \frac{d}{2h_B} = 0.208
  6. State the result: μs=0.208\mu_s = 0.208 at minimum. The mass cancels, so the answer depends only on the geometry.

Full solution

Given: m=14 kgm = 14\ \mathrm{kg}, L=6.5 mL = 6.5\ \mathrm{m}, d=2.5 md = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}, smooth wall, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Find the height of BB above the floor from the right triangle: hB=L2−d2=(6.5 m)2−(2.5 m)2=6.00 mh_B = \sqrt{L^2 - d^2} = \sqrt{(6.5\ \mathrm{m})^2 - (2.5\ \mathrm{m})^2} = 6.00\ \mathrm{m}

2. Compute the weight, which acts at midlength, a horizontal distance d/2d/2 from AA: W=mg=(14 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=137.3 NW = mg = (14\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 137.3\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply ∑MA=0\sum M_A = 0; the smooth wall exerts only a horizontal force NBN_B: W(d2)−NB hB=0  ⇒  NB=(137.3 N)(1.25 m)6.00 m=28.61 NW\left(\frac{d}{2}\right) - N_B\,h_B = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; N_B = \frac{(137.3\ \mathrm{N})(1.25\ \mathrm{m})}{6.00\ \mathrm{m}} = 28.61\ \mathrm{N}

4. Apply ∑Fx=0\sum F_x = 0 and ∑Fy=0\sum F_y = 0: FA=NB=28.61 N,NA=W=137.3 NF_A = N_B = 28.61\ \mathrm{N}, \qquad N_A = W = 137.3\ \mathrm{N}

5. Require FA≤μsNAF_A \le \mu_s N_A; the minimum coefficient is μs=FANA=28.61 N137.3 N=d2hB=0.208\mu_s = \frac{F_A}{N_A} = \frac{28.61\ \mathrm{N}}{137.3\ \mathrm{N}} = \frac{d}{2h_B} = 0.208

6. State the result: μs=0.208\mu_s = 0.208 at minimum. The mass cancels, so the answer depends only on the geometry.

Answer: 0.208

7. Friction on an incline

Set a block on a ramp at angle θ. Choose axes along the slope and perpendicular to it. The weight then has a component W sin θ down the slope and a component W cos θ into it. With nothing else acting, equilibrium gives:

F = W sin θ,   N = W cos θ

While the block holds, the friction force is W sin θ. It is not μsN until the block is about to slip. At that point W sin θ = μsW cos θ, the weight cancels, and

tan φs = μs φs is the angle of static friction

This is how a coefficient of friction is measured: tilt the surface until the block lets go. A block can also tip on a ramp. With base b and height H, it tips when its weight’s line of action passes the downhill edge of the base, at tan θ = b/H. Whichever angle is smaller is reached first.

When another force acts along the slope, find the direction of friction the usual way: ask which way the block would slide without it. A block held from sliding down has friction pointing up the slope. A block being pushed up has friction pointing down the slope.

Try it: the window of forces that hold

A block on a steep ramp is held by a force along the slope. Too little and it slides down. Too much and it slides up. In between, friction quietly changes size and direction to make up the difference. Find both ends of the window, then see how the window changes with μs.

In class: inclines

Problem 13Block at rest on an incline

A block of mass m=12 kgm = 12\ \mathrm{kg} rests without moving on a board inclined at θ=15∘\theta = 15^{\circ} to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the board is μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the friction force actually acting on the block.

Answer 30.5 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(12)(9.81)=117.72 NW = (12)(9.81) = 117.72\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Recognize that motion is not impending, so FF comes from equilibrium, not from μsN\mu_s N.
  3. Sum forces along the incline: F−Wsin⁡θ=0F - W\sin\theta = 0.
  4. Substitute: F=(117.72)sin⁡15∘=30.47 NF = (117.72)\sin 15^{\circ} = 30.47\ \mathrm{N}
  5. Check the limit: Fmax=μsWcos⁡θ=(0.40)(113.71)=45.5 NF_{max} = \mu_s W\cos\theta = (0.40)(113.71) = 45.5\ \mathrm{N}, which is larger than FF.
  6. State the result: F≈30.5 NF \approx 30.5\ \mathrm{N}, directed up the slope.

Full solution

Given: m=12 kgm = 12\ \mathrm{kg}, θ=15∘\theta = 15^{\circ}, μs=0.40\mu_s = 0.40. W=(12)(9.81)=117.72 NW = (12)(9.81) = 117.72\ \mathrm{N}. The block is at rest and nothing says motion is impending, so friction is found from equilibrium, not from μsN\mu_s N. Along the incline: F−Wsin⁡θ=0F - W\sin\theta = 0, so F=Wsin⁡θ=(117.72 N)sin⁡15∘=30.47 N≈30.5 NF = W\sin\theta = (117.72\ \mathrm{N})\sin 15^{\circ} = 30.47\ \mathrm{N} \approx 30.5\ \mathrm{N} Check: N=Wcos⁡θ=113.71 NN = W\cos\theta = 113.71\ \mathrm{N} and Fmax=(0.40)(113.71)=45.5 NF_{max} = (0.40)(113.71) = 45.5\ \mathrm{N}. Since 30.5 N≤45.5 N30.5\ \mathrm{N} \le 45.5\ \mathrm{N}, the block does stay at rest.

Problem 10Block on a tilting board at the angle of static friction

A block is placed on a flat board, and the board is slowly tilted. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the board is μs=0.36\mu_s = 0.36. The block is short and wide, so it will slip rather than tip.

Determine the angle of static friction ϕs\phi_s, the incline angle at which slipping is impending.

Answer 19.8 deg

Steps

  1. Resolve the weight on the incline: F=Wsin⁡ϕF = W\sin\phi along the surface and N=Wcos⁡ϕN = W\cos\phi normal to it.
  2. Apply the impending-slip condition: F=μsNF = \mu_s N.
  3. Combine: Wsin⁡ϕs=μsWcos⁡ϕs⇒tan⁡ϕs=μsW\sin\phi_s = \mu_s W\cos\phi_s \Rightarrow \tan\phi_s = \mu_s
  4. Substitute: ϕs=tan⁡−1(0.36)\phi_s = \tan^{-1}(0.36)
  5. State the result: ϕs≈19.8∘\phi_s \approx 19.8^{\circ}.

Full solution

Given: μs=0.36\mu_s = 0.36. On an incline at angle ϕ\phi, equilibrium along and perpendicular to the surface gives F=Wsin⁡ϕF = W\sin\phi and N=Wcos⁡ϕN = W\cos\phi. At impending slip F=μsNF = \mu_s N, so Wsin⁡ϕs=μsWcos⁡ϕsW\sin\phi_s = \mu_s W\cos\phi_s and tan⁡ϕs=μs⇒ϕs=tan⁡−1(0.36)=19.8∘\tan\phi_s = \mu_s \Rightarrow \phi_s = \tan^{-1}(0.36) = 19.8^{\circ} The weight cancels, so the result does not depend on the block’s mass.

Problem 15Tall crate on a ramp of increasing angle

A uniform rectangular crate has a base of width a=0.40 ma = 0.40\ \mathrm{m} and a height H=1.20 mH = 1.20\ \mathrm{m}. It stands on a ramp whose angle θ\theta with the horizontal is slowly increased. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the ramp is μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45. No other forces act on the crate.

Determine the smallest ramp angle θ\theta at which the crate is on the verge of motion, and identify whether it slips or tips.

Answer 18.4 deg

Steps

  1. Resolve the weight on the ramp: F=Wsin⁡θF = W\sin\theta and N=Wcos⁡θN = W\cos\theta.
  2. Assume slipping, F=μsNF = \mu_s N: tan⁡θslip=0.45⇒θslip=24.2∘\tan\theta_{slip} = 0.45 \Rightarrow \theta_{slip} = 24.2^{\circ}
  3. Assume tipping: NN acts at the downhill edge of the base.
  4. Take moments about that edge: (Wsin⁡θ)H2=(Wcos⁡θ)a2(W\sin\theta)\frac{H}{2} = (W\cos\theta)\frac{a}{2}
  5. Solve: tan⁡θtip=aH=0.401.20⇒θtip=18.4∘\tan\theta_{tip} = \frac{a}{H} = \frac{0.40}{1.20} \Rightarrow \theta_{tip} = 18.4^{\circ}
  6. Compare: tipping occurs at the smaller angle, and the slip check 0.333≤0.450.333 \le 0.45 passes.
  7. State the result: motion is impending at θ≈18.4∘\theta \approx 18.4^{\circ}, and the crate tips.

Full solution

Given: a=0.40 ma = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}, H=1.20 mH = 1.20\ \mathrm{m}, μs=0.45\mu_s = 0.45. Assume slipping: F=Wsin⁡θF = W\sin\theta, N=Wcos⁡θN = W\cos\theta, and F=μsNF = \mu_s N give tan⁡θ=μs\tan\theta = \mu_s, so θslip=tan⁡−1(0.45)=24.2∘\theta_{slip} = \tan^{-1}(0.45) = 24.2^{\circ}. Assume tipping: NN acts at the downhill edge, so the line of action of WW through GG passes through that edge. Moments about the downhill edge: (Wsin⁡θ)(H/2)=(Wcos⁡θ)(a/2)(W\sin\theta)(H/2) = (W\cos\theta)(a/2), so tan⁡θ=aH=0.40 m1.20 m=0.3333,θtip=18.4∘\tan\theta = \frac{a}{H} = \frac{0.40\ \mathrm{m}}{1.20\ \mathrm{m}} = 0.3333, \quad \theta_{tip} = 18.4^{\circ} The smaller angle governs. Check at 18.4∘18.4^{\circ}: required F/N=tan⁡θ=0.333≤0.45F/N = \tan\theta = 0.333 \le 0.45, so the crate has not slipped. The crate tips at θ≈18.4∘\theta \approx 18.4^{\circ}.

Problem 20Holding force on a block that tends to slide down a ramp

A block of mass m=15 kgm = 15\ \mathrm{kg} sits on a ramp inclined at θ=35∘\theta = 35^{\circ} to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is μs=0.25\mu_s = 0.25, which is too small to hold the block by itself. A force PP is applied parallel to the ramp, directed up the slope, to keep the block from sliding down. Use g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Determine the smallest force PP that prevents the block from sliding down the ramp.

Answer 54.3 N

Steps

  1. Compute the weight: W=(15)(9.81)=147.15 NW = (15)(9.81) = 147.15\ \mathrm{N}
  2. Set the friction direction: the block tends to slide down, so FF points up the slope.
  3. Sum forces perpendicular to the ramp: N=Wcos⁡35∘=120.54 NN = W\cos 35^{\circ} = 120.54\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Sum forces along the ramp: P+F−Wsin⁡θ=0P + F - W\sin\theta = 0.
  5. Use impending slip, F=μsNF = \mu_s N: P=W(sin⁡θ−μscos⁡θ)P = W(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta)
  6. Substitute: P=(147.15)(0.5736−0.2048)=54.27 NP = (147.15)(0.5736 - 0.2048) = 54.27\ \mathrm{N}
  7. State the result: P≈54.3 NP \approx 54.3\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=15 kgm = 15\ \mathrm{kg}, θ=35∘\theta = 35^{\circ}, μs=0.25\mu_s = 0.25. W=(15)(9.81)=147.15 NW = (15)(9.81) = 147.15\ \mathrm{N}. For the smallest PP, the block is about to slide down, so friction acts up the slope at its maximum value. Perpendicular to the ramp: N=Wcos⁡θ=(147.15)(0.8192)=120.54 NN = W\cos\theta = (147.15)(0.8192) = 120.54\ \mathrm{N}. Along the ramp: P+F−Wsin⁡θ=0P + F - W\sin\theta = 0 with F=μsNF = \mu_s N: P=W(sin⁡θ−μscos⁡θ)=(147.15 N)(0.5736−0.2048)=54.27 N≈54.3 NP = W(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta) = (147.15\ \mathrm{N})(0.5736 - 0.2048) = 54.27\ \mathrm{N} \approx 54.3\ \mathrm{N}

Impending motion is up the slope, so friction on the block points down the slope. Perpendicular to the ramp: N=Wcos⁡θ=(176.58)(0.9397)=165.93 NN = W\cos\theta = (176.58)(0.9397) = 165.93\ \mathrm{N}. Along the ramp: P−Wsin⁡θ−F=0P - W\sin\theta - F = 0 with F=μsNF = \mu_s N: P=W(sin⁡θ+μscos⁡θ)=(176.58 N)(0.3420+0.2819)=110.2 N≈110 NP = W(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta) = (176.58\ \mathrm{N})(0.3420 + 0.2819) = 110.2\ \mathrm{N} \approx 110\ \mathrm{N}

Steps

  6. Check: at θslip\theta_{slip}, tan⁡θ=0.40<a/H=0.4545\tan\theta = 0.40 < a/H = 0.4545, so the normal force is still inside the base and the crate has not tipped.
  7. State the result: the crate first moves at θ=21.8∘\theta = 21.8^{\circ}, and it slips.

Set 2, Problem 20Holding force on a block that tends to slide down

A block of mass m=24 kgm = 24\ \mathrm{kg} sits on a rough incline at θ=40∘\theta = 40^{\circ} to the horizontal, where μs=0.30\mu_s = 0.30. Steps

  2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(24 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=235.4 NW = mg = (24\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 235.4\ \mathrm{N}

Full solution

Given: m=24 kgm = 24\ \mathrm{kg}, θ=40∘\theta = 40^{\circ}, μs=0.30\mu_s = 0.30, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Set the friction direction: at the smallest PP the block is about to slide down, so friction acts up the slope and helps PP, with F=μsNF = \mu_s N.

2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(24 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=235.4 NW = mg = (24\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 235.4\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply equilibrium perpendicular to the slope: N=Wcos⁡θ=(235.4 N)cos⁡40∘=180.4 NN = W\cos\theta = (235.4\ \mathrm{N})\cos 40^{\circ} = 180.4\ \mathrm{N}

4. Apply equilibrium along the slope: P+μsN−Wsin⁡θ=0  ⇒  P=W(sin⁡θ−μscos⁡θ)P + \mu_s N - W\sin\theta = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P = W(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta)

5. Substitute: P=(235.4 N)sin⁡40∘−(0.30)(180.4 N)=151.3 N−54.11 N=97.23 NP = (235.4\ \mathrm{N})\sin 40^{\circ} - (0.30)(180.4\ \mathrm{N}) = 151.3\ \mathrm{N} - 54.11\ \mathrm{N} = 97.23\ \mathrm{N}

6. State the result: P=97.2 NP = 97.2\ \mathrm{N}.

Answer: 97.2 N97.2\ \mathrm{N}

Set 2, Problem 21Force to start a block moving up a ramp

A block of mass m=26 kgm = 26\ \mathrm{kg} rests on a rough ramp inclined at θ=24∘\theta = 24^{\circ} to the horizontal, where μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35. A force PP parallel to the ramp and directed up the slope is applied, as shown. Take g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. Determine the magnitude of PP required to bring the block to the verge of moving up the ramp.

Determine the force PP for impending motion up the ramp.

Answer 185 N

Steps

  1. Set the friction direction: the block is about to move up the ramp, so friction acts down the slope and opposes PP, with F=μsNF = \mu_s N.
  2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(26 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=255.1 NW = mg = (26\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 255.1\ \mathrm{N}
  3. Apply equilibrium perpendicular to the slope: N=Wcos⁡θ=(255.1 N)cos⁡24∘=233.0 NN = W\cos\theta = (255.1\ \mathrm{N})\cos 24^{\circ} = 233.0\ \mathrm{N}
  4. Apply equilibrium along the slope: P−Wsin⁡θ−μsN=0  ⇒  P=W(sin⁡θ+μscos⁡θ)P - W\sin\theta - \mu_s N = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P = W(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta)
  5. Substitute: P=(255.1 N)sin⁡24∘+(0.35)(233.0 N)=103.7 N+81.55 N=185.3 NP = (255.1\ \mathrm{N})\sin 24^{\circ} + (0.35)(233.0\ \mathrm{N}) = 103.7\ \mathrm{N} + 81.55\ \mathrm{N} = 185.3\ \mathrm{N}
  6. State the result: P=185 NP = 185\ \mathrm{N}.

Full solution

Given: m=26 kgm = 26\ \mathrm{kg}, θ=24∘\theta = 24^{\circ}, μs=0.35\mu_s = 0.35, g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Solution:

1. Set the friction direction: the block is about to move up the ramp, so friction acts down the slope and opposes PP, with F=μsNF = \mu_s N.

2. Compute the weight: W=mg=(26 kg)(9.81 m/s2)=255.1 NW = mg = (26\ \mathrm{kg})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 255.1\ \mathrm{N}

3. Apply equilibrium perpendicular to the slope: N=Wcos⁡θ=(255.1 N)cos⁡24∘=233.0 NN = W\cos\theta = (255.1\ \mathrm{N})\cos 24^{\circ} = 233.0\ \mathrm{N}

4. Apply equilibrium along the slope: P−Wsin⁡θ−μsN=0  ⇒  P=W(sin⁡θ+μscos⁡θ)P - W\sin\theta - \mu_s N = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P = W(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta)

5. Substitute: P=(255.1 N)sin⁡24∘+(0.35)(233.0 N)=103.7 N+81.55 N=185.3 NP = (255.1\ \mathrm{N})\sin 24^{\circ} + (0.35)(233.0\ \mathrm{N}) = 103.7\ \mathrm{N} + 81.55\ \mathrm{N} = 185.3\ \mathrm{N}

6. State the result: P=185 NP = 185\ \mathrm{N}.

Answer: 185 N185\ \mathrm{N}

8. Friction in unexpected places

Crates and ladders are where friction problems start. These three are where the same two ideas, F ≤ μsN and the angle of static friction, turn up in the world, and each one behaves in a way most people do not expect.

A rope around a post: holding a ship with one hand

A dock worker takes a few turns of rope around a bollard and holds back a ship. A climber’s belay device, a sailor’s winch, and a cowboy’s turn around the saddle horn all work the same way. Each small length of rope presses on the post, the friction there carries part of the tension, and what is left presses the next length a little less hard. The tension falls off like compound interest in reverse:

Thold = Tload e−μsβ β is the angle of wrap in radians; one full turn is 2π

Notice what is missing. The size of the post does not appear, and neither does the length of rope in contact. Only the angle of wrap and the coefficient of friction matter (Hibbeler, 2022). With μs = 0.30, three turns reduce a 20 kN pull to (20 000 N)e−(0.30)(6π) = 70 N, about the weight of a 7-kg bag.

Predict before you try it: does going from two turns to four halve the holding force, or do something much more drastic?

A wedge that cannot be squeezed out

A doorstop, a shim under a machine, and the taper on a drill chuck all stay put under load with nothing holding them. So does every screw and bolt, because a thread is a wedge wrapped around a cylinder. The reason is the angle of static friction from Section 7. The contact force on each face of the wedge can lean away from the normal by at most φs, where tan φs = μs. For a light wedge with the same friction on both faces, the forces on its two faces can balance each other only if

α ≤ 2φs α is the wedge angle; a wedge that meets this is called self-locking

The load does not appear in that condition. A heavier load pushes the wedge sideways harder, and presses its faces together harder by exactly the same proportion. A self-locking wedge holds any load; a wedge that is too steep holds none. With μs = 0.25, φs = 14.0°, so a wedge up to 28.1° locks.

A climber in a chimney: held up by pushing sideways

A climber can rest in a vertical crack with nothing underneath, back against one wall and feet against the other. Nothing pushes up on the climber except friction, and friction exists only because the climber pushes outward. Summing vertical forces, the two friction forces must carry the weight, and each is limited by its own coefficient:

W ≤ (μ1 + μ2)N,   so   N ≥ W/(μ1 + μ2)

The same equation describes lifting a stack of books by pressing on its ends, ice tongs, and a brake caliper squeezing a rotor. For a 70-kg climber with μ1 = 0.60 at the shoes and μ2 = 0.40 at the back, N ≥ (687 N)/(1.00) = 687 N: the climber must push sideways with a force equal to their own weight. On wet rock the coefficients might halve, and the push needed doubles.

Note. The three figures in this section are interactive and original. The chimney model treats the climber as a rigid body in vertical force balance and does not show how the friction is shared between the two walls before slipping, which equilibrium alone cannot determine.

Summary

  • Static friction is a reaction. It equals whatever equilibrium requires, up to μsN.
  • Write F = μsN only when motion is impending. Otherwise, solve for F and check it.
  • Friction opposes sliding between surfaces, which is not always the direction opposite the body’s motion.
  • On a rigid body, N shifts toward the edge the body would tip about. Tipping is impending when N reaches that edge.
  • When slipping and tipping are both possible, assume one, solve, and check the other.
  • Get N from equilibrium every time. An angled force or a slope changes it.
  • On an incline with no other forces, slipping is impending when tan θ = μs.
  • A rope wrapped around a post loses tension exponentially with the angle of wrap, and a wedge thinner than twice the angle of static friction locks under any load.
  • For a crate pushed horizontally, the comparison comes down to μs against a/(2h). The smaller one is reached first.

Key terms

Dry (Coulomb) friction
Friction between unlubricated solid surfaces.
Normal force, N
The resultant contact force perpendicular to the surface.
Static friction force, F
The tangential force that prevents sliding. It takes whatever value equilibrium requires, up to a limit: F ≤ μsN.
Maximum static friction, Fmax
μsN, reached only at impending motion.
Impending motion
The state in which a body is on the verge of slipping.
Kinetic friction force, Fk
μkN, acting while surfaces slide.
Coefficients of static and kinetic friction, μs and μk
Dimensionless ratios that depend on the pair of surfaces. Typically μs is greater than μk.
Slipping
Sliding at the contact surface.
Tipping
Rotation about an edge, which begins when the normal force reaches that edge (x = a/2 for a base of width a).
Angle of static friction, φs
The incline angle at impending slip, where tan φs = μs. You will use this in the lab.
Angle of wrap, β
The angle, in radians, over which a rope or belt touches a post or pulley. One full turn is 2π.
Self-locking
Describes a wedge or screw that stays in place under load with no holding force, because its angle is small compared with the angle of static friction.
